title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter VIII
paragraphs:
“Oh, rescue her! I am her brother now,
And you her father. Every gentle maid
Should have a guardian in each gentleman.”

Sir James Chettam was surprised how much he still enjoyed visiting the Grange once he had faced the first difficulty of seeing Dorothea as a woman engaged to someone else. Naturally, forked lightning seemed to shoot through him when he first approached her, and throughout the visit he knew he was concealing distress. Yet good as he was, we must admit that he suffered less than he would have if he had considered his rival a brilliant and desirable match. He did not feel eclipsed by Mr. Casaubon, only shocked that Dorothea laboured under a sad delusion. Compassion mingled with his humiliation and took away some of its bitterness.

Still, though Sir James told himself he had entirely given her up—since, with Desdemona's perversity, she had rejected a prospective match so plainly suitable and natural—he could not yet passively accept her engagement to Mr. Casaubon. The first day he saw them together with his new knowledge, he felt he had not taken the matter seriously enough. Brooke was truly at fault; he ought to have prevented it. Who could speak to him? Perhaps even now something could be done, at least to postpone the wedding. On the way home he turned into the Rectory and asked for Mr. Cadwallader. Fortunately the Rector was in. Sir James was shown into the study, where all the fishing tackle hung. Mr. Cadwallader himself was working at his lathe in a small adjoining room and called him through. These two were closer friends than any other landowner and clergyman in the county, a significant fact in keeping with the kindly expressions on their faces.

Mr. Cadwallader was a large man with full lips and a sweet smile, very plain and rough-looking, but possessed of an unshakeable ease and good humour that spread to those around him. Like great grassy hills in sunlight, they soothed even an irritated self-importance and made it a little ashamed. “Well, how are you?” he asked, showing a hand not quite fit to shake. “Sorry I missed you earlier. Anything particular? You look annoyed.”
A small crease marked Sir James's brow, a slight lowering of the eyebrows that he seemed deliberately to deepen as he replied.
“It's just this behaviour of Brooke's. I really believe someone ought to speak to him.”

“What, his plan to stand for Parliament?” Mr. Cadwallader asked, continuing to arrange the reels he had just made on the lathe. “I doubt he means it. But where's the harm if he wants to? Anyone opposed to the Whigs should be glad they aren't putting forward their strongest man. They won't knock down the Constitution using our friend Brooke's head as a battering ram.”

“Oh, I don't mean that,” Sir James said. He had put his hat down and dropped into a chair, where he clasped his leg and bitterly examined the sole of his boot. “I mean this marriage. Letting that lovely young girl marry Casaubon.”
“What's wrong with Casaubon? I know no harm of him, if the girl likes him.”

“She's too young to know what she likes. Her guardian should intervene. He shouldn't let it be rushed through like this. I'm surprised a man like you, Cadwallader, a man with daughters, can regard it indifferently—and with your kind heart! Do consider it seriously.”

“I'm not joking. I couldn't be more serious,” the Rector said with an irritating little inward chuckle. “You're as bad as Elinor. She's been urging me to lecture Brooke, and I've reminded her that her friends thought very poorly of her own match when she married me.”
“But look at Casaubon,” Sir James protested indignantly. “He must be fifty, and I doubt he's ever been much more than a man's shadow. Just look at his legs!”

“Damn you handsome young fellows! You expect everything in the world to go your way. You don't understand women. They admire you half as much as you admire yourselves. Elinor used to tell her sisters she'd married me for my ugliness: it was so varied and entertaining it overcame all her prudence.”
“You! Loving you would be easy for any woman. But looks aren't the issue. I don't _like_ Casaubon.” This was Sir James's strongest way of suggesting a poor opinion of someone's character.
“Why? What do you know against him?” The Rector set down his reels and hooked his thumbs into his waistcoat armholes, looking attentive.
Sir James hesitated. Explaining his reasons was seldom easy for him. Since he felt only what was reasonable, it seemed strange that other people should need to be told. At last he said—
“Come now, Cadwallader, does he have any heart?”

“Well, yes. Not a melting one, I don't mean that, but a sound core—you can rely on _that_. He's very good to his poor relations. He pays pensions to several of the women and spends a good deal educating a young man. Casaubon lives by his sense of justice. His mother's sister married badly—a Pole, I think—and lost her place in society; anyway, her family disowned her. Without that, Casaubon wouldn't have half so much money. I believe he sought his cousins out himself to see what he could do. Not every man would ring as true as that if you tested his metal. _You_ would, Chettam, but not everyone.”

“I don't know,” Sir James said, reddening. “I'm not so certain of myself.” After a pause he added, “Casaubon did the right thing there. But a man can want to act rightly and still be a sort of legal code on parchment. A woman might not be happy with him. And when a girl is as young as Miss Brooke, I think her friends should intervene a little to keep her from doing something foolish. You're laughing because you imagine I'm thinking of myself. But on my honour, that isn't it. I'd feel exactly the same if I were her brother or her uncle.”
“Well, then, what would you actually do?”
“I'd insist the marriage couldn't be settled until she came of age. And believe me, in that case it would never happen. I wish you saw it my way. I wish you'd talk to Brooke.”

Sir James stood as he finished, seeing Mrs. Cadwallader enter from the study. She held her youngest daughter's hand. The child, about five, ran straight to papa, who settled her comfortably on his knee.

“I can hear what you're discussing,” his wife said. “But you won't influence Humphrey. As long as the fish take his bait, everyone is exactly as they should be. Bless you, Casaubon owns a trout stream and doesn't want to fish it himself. Could anyone be a better fellow?”
“Well, there's something to that,” the Rector said with his quiet inward laugh. “Owning a trout stream is a very good quality in a man.”
“But seriously,” Sir James persisted, his irritation still unspent, “don't you think the Rector might help if he spoke up?”
“Oh, I warned you what he'd say,” Mrs. Cadwallader answered, raising her eyebrows. “I've done what I can. I wash my hands of this marriage.”

“First of all,” the Rector said, becoming rather serious, “it would be absurd to expect me to convince Brooke and get him to act on it. He's a very good fellow, but soft as pulp. He'll flow into any mould, but he won't hold the shape.”
“He might hold it long enough to postpone the wedding,” Sir James replied.

“But my dear Chettam, why should I use my influence against Casaubon unless I were far more certain than I am that it would benefit Miss Brooke? I know nothing bad about him. His Xisuthrus and Fee-fo-fum and all the rest don't interest me, but then my fishing tackle doesn't interest him. His position on the Catholic Question surprised me, but he's always been civil, and I see no reason to spoil his sport. For all I know, Miss Brooke could be happier with him than with any other man.”
“Humphrey! You try my patience. You know perfectly well you'd rather eat dinner under a hedge than alone with Casaubon. You've nothing to say to each other.”
“What has that to do with Miss Brooke marrying him? She isn't doing it to entertain me.”
“There isn't any healthy red blood in his body,” Sir James declared.
“No. Someone examined a drop through a magnifying glass and found nothing but semicolons and parentheses,” Mrs. Cadwallader replied.
“Why doesn't he publish his book instead of getting married?” Sir James asked, with a disgust he considered justified by an English layman's sound instincts.

“Oh, he dreams in footnotes, and they carry off all his brains. They say he made an abstract of ‘Hop o' my Thumb’ as a little boy, and he's been making abstracts ever since. Ugh! And Humphrey keeps saying a woman could be happy with that man.”
“Well, Miss Brooke likes him,” said the Rector. “I don't claim to understand every young lady's preferences.”
“But suppose she was your own daughter?” Sir James asked.

“Then it would be different. She _isn't_ my daughter, and I don't feel obliged to interfere. Casaubon's as good as most of us. He's a learned clergyman who does credit to his profession. Some Radical making a speech in Middlemarch called him the incumbent who chopped learned straw, Freke the bricks-and-mortar incumbent, and me the fishing incumbent. On my word, I can't see that one is better or worse than another.” The Rector finished with his silent chuckle. He always appreciated the joke in satire directed at himself. Like the rest of him, his conscience was large and comfortable: it did only what caused it no trouble.

Plainly Mr. Cadwallader would not obstruct Miss Brooke's marriage. Sir James sadly felt she was to have complete freedom to misjudge. His good nature showed in the fact that he never slackened his intention to carry out Dorothea's cottage scheme. Doubtless persistence best preserved his dignity, but pride only helps us act generously; it no more creates generosity than vanity creates wit. Dorothea now understood enough of his feelings to value the integrity with which he continued a landlord's duty first undertaken from a lover's eagerness to please. Her pleasure in it was strong enough to matter even amid her present happiness. Perhaps Sir James's cottages received all the interest she could spare from Mr. Casaubon—or rather from the symphony of hopeful dreams, admiring trust and passionate devotion that the learned gentleman had set playing in her soul. Thus, on later visits, while the good baronet began offering Celia small attentions, he found himself talking to Dorothea with increasing pleasure. She was now entirely relaxed and free from irritation with him. Gradually he discovered the delight of candid kindness and companionship between a man and woman who have no passion either to conceal or confess.
